'''Larry L. Taylor''' (12 February 1942 – 28 January 2024) was a [[United States Army]] officer and helicopter pilot who was awarded the [[Medal of Honor]] on 5 September 2023 for his actions on 18 June 1968 during the [[Vietnam War]].

==Early life and education==
Taylor was born on 12 February 1942 and raised in [[Chattanooga, Tennessee]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Larry L. Taylor {{!}} Vietnam War {{!}} U.S. Army {{!}} Medal of Honor Recipient |url=https://www.cmohs.org/recipients/larry-l-taylor |website=Congressional Medal of Honor Society |access-date=3 February 2024 |language=en}}</ref> and attended the [[University of Tennessee]] in [[Knoxville, Tennessee|Knoxville]], where he served in the [[Reserve Officers' Training Corps]].<ref name=Chat>{{cite web|url=https://www.chattanoogan.com/2023/7/9/471613/Larry-Taylor-Gets-The-Call-From.aspx|title=Larry Taylor Gets The Call From President Biden|publisher=Chattanoogan.com|author=Earl Freudenberg|date=9 July 2023|access-date=8 August 2023|archive-date=10 August 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810225114/https://www.chattanoogan.com/2023/7/9/471613/Larry-Taylor-Gets-The-Call-From.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>

Following his graduation in June 1966, Taylor attended the [[United States Army Armor School]] at [[Fort Knox]], then trained on helicopters at [[Fort Wolters]] and then [[Fort Rucker]], graduating as an army aviator on 30 June 1967.<ref name="Chat" /><ref name="White">{{cite web |date=1 September 2023 |title=President Joseph R. Biden, Jr. to Award the Medal of Honor |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/09/01/president-joseph-r-biden-jr-to-award-the-medal-of-honor-3/ |access-date=5 September 2023 |publisher=The White House |archive-date=5 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230905061708/https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2023/09/01/president-joseph-r-biden-jr-to-award-the-medal-of-honor-3/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Military career==
Taylor was sent to [[South Vietnam]] in August 1967 joining D Troop, 1st Squadron, [[4th Cavalry Regiment (United States)|4th Cavalry Regiment]], part of the [[1st Infantry Division (United States)|1st Infantry Division]], at [[Bien Hoa Air Base]].<ref name=Chat/>

On the night of 18 June 1968, Taylor, together with his gunner [[Warrant officer (United States)|CWO2]] J. O. Ratliff, rescued a four-man [[long-range reconnaissance patrol]] (LRRP) that had been surrounded by [[Vietcong]] forces near the village of Ap Go Cong, [[Bình Dương province]].<ref name=Chat/> After exhausting his munitions, Taylor (callsign ''Darkhorse 32'') landed his [[Bell AH-1 Cobra|AH-1G Cobra]] and the four LRRP soldiers clung to the skids and rocket pods of the helicopter as Taylor flew them to safety. For his actions, Taylor was originally awarded the [[Silver Star]]. His Silver Star was upgraded to the [[Medal of Honor]] in 2023.<ref name=White/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://foxchattanooga.com/news/local/vietnam-veteran-from-chattanooga-will-be-awarded-the-medal-of-honor|title=Vietnam Veteran from Chattanooga will be awarded the Medal of Honor|publisher=Fox Chattanooga|author=Josh Roe|date=9 July 2023|access-date=9 August 2023|archive-date=10 August 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810230123/https://foxchattanooga.com/news/local/vietnam-veteran-from-chattanooga-will-be-awarded-the-medal-of-honor|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.yahoo.com/daring-vietnam-rescue-finally-results-180604105.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAADozVG-H__5Qoer4_ITAhi-cVCEHo14Kws-ywjE1J6ZVOgqPIzu-iV8mRJqmL1L1Gdtd5klRsi4cP6KVHbF7zH6Z7_inJ3T9s6OjAwPz2m3IMbsRvw5PB6ShWXnGKrFopdXQTdfujN2HQu1ps25iLDylOzpjQFMNKQaHvCBJKip4|title=This daring Vietnam rescue finally results in Medal of Honor award|publisher=Yahoo News|author=Todd South|date=1 September 2023|access-date=6 September 2023|archive-date=6 September 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230906034451/https://news.yahoo.com/daring-vietnam-rescue-finally-results-180604105.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAADozVG-H__5Qoer4_ITAhi-cVCEHo14Kws-ywjE1J6ZVOgqPIzu-iV8mRJqmL1L1Gdtd5klRsi4cP6KVHbF7zH6Z7_inJ3T9s6OjAwPz2m3IMbsRvw5PB6ShWXnGKrFopdXQTdfujN2HQu1ps25iLDylOzpjQFMNKQaHvCBJKip4|url-status=live}}</ref>

Taylor flew over 2,000 combat missions during the [[Vietnam War]] in the Cobra and the [[Bell UH-1 Iroquois|UH-1]], was engaged by enemy fire 340 times and was shot down five times.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2023/09/05/politics/medal-of-honor-larry-taylor-vietnam/index.html|title=Helicopter pilot receives Medal of Honor for daring rescue during Vietnam War|publisher=CNN|author=Haley Britzky|date=5 September 2023|access-date=6 September 2023|archive-date=6 September 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230906031705/https://edition.cnn.com/2023/09/05/politics/medal-of-honor-larry-taylor-vietnam/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Following his Vietnam service, he served in the [[2nd Cavalry Regiment (United States)|2nd Cavalry Regiment]] in [[West Germany]].<ref name=Chat/>

Taylor left active duty in 1971 with the rank of [[Captain (United States O-3)|Captain]].<ref name=Chat/>

==Death==
Taylor died at his home in Signal Mountain, Tennessee, on 28 January 2024, at the age of 81,<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Nicholson |first1=Ken |url=https://www.local3news.com/local-news/medal-of-honor-recipient-captain-larry-taylor-of-signal-mountain-passes-away-at-age-81/article_ae7c7666-bebc-11ee-8c4c-bf5472fc0db5.html |title=Medal of Honor recipient Captain Larry Taylor of Signal Mountain passes away at age 81 |date=29 January 2024 |access-date=2 February 2024 |archive-date=29 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240129192251/https://www.local3news.com/local-news/medal-of-honor-recipient-captain-larry-taylor-of-signal-mountain-passes-away-at-age-81/article_ae7c7666-bebc-11ee-8c4c-bf5472fc0db5.html |url-status=live |publisher=[[WRCB]], Local3}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Congressional Medal of Honor Society Announces Passing of Medal of Honor Recipient Larry L. Taylor|author=Congressional Medal of Honor Society|publisher=PR Newswire|url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/congressional-medal-of-honor-society-announces-passing-of-medal-of-honor-recipient-larry-l-taylor-302047007.html|date=29 January 2024|access-date=31 January 2024|archive-date=31 January 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240131185408/https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/congressional-medal-of-honor-society-announces-passing-of-medal-of-honor-recipient-larry-l-taylor-302047007.html|url-status=live}}</ref> after "a long struggle with cancer".<ref>{{cite news |title=Recent Congressional Medal Of Honor Recipient Capt. Larry Taylor Dies At 81 |url=https://www.chattanoogan.com/2024/1/29/481795/Recent-Congressional-Medal-Of-Honor.aspx |access-date=3 February 2024 |publisher=www.chattanoogan.com |date=30 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Taylor's personal decorations include: the Medal of Honor (upgraded in 2023 from a Silver Star awarded 1968<ref name="Chat" />), [[Distinguished Flying Cross (United States)|Distinguished Flying Cross]] (4), [[Bronze Star Medal]], [[Air Medal]] (43), and the [[Republic of Vietnam Gallantry Cross]], with 2 bronze stars.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://alumni.utk.edu/s/1341/2./20/interior.aspx?sid=1341&gid=2&pgid=19404&cid=38480&ecid=38480&crid=0&calpgid=8907&calcid=38473|title=Larry L. Taylor ('66)|publisher=University of Tennessee, Knoxville|access-date=9 August 2023}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

===Medal of Honor citation===
{{quotebox

|[[File:Moh army mil.jpg|130px|center]]

<blockquote>The President of the United States of America, authorized by Act of [[United States Congress|Congress]], March 3rd, 1863, has awarded in the name of Congress the [[Medal of Honor]] to First Lieutenant Larry L. Taylor, United States Army, for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty.

[[First Lieutenant]] Larry L. Taylor distinguished himself by acts of gallantry and intrepidity above and beyond the call of duty while serving with Troop Delta, 1st Squadron, 4th Cavalry, 1st Infantry Division on June 18th, 1968, near the village of Ap Go Cong, Republic of Vietnam.

On this date, First Lieutenant Taylor commanded a light fire team of two Cobra helicopter gunships scrambled on a nighttime mission in response to an urgent call for aerial fire support from a four-man, long-range patrol team.

Upon arrival, First Lieutenant Taylor found the patrol team surrounded and heavily engaged by a larger Viet Cong force. He immediately requested illumination rounds and supporting artillery to assist with identifying the enemy positions.

Despite intense enemy groundfire, he flew at a perilously low altitude, placing a devastating volume of aerial rocket and machine gun fire on the enemy forces encircling the friendly patrol.

For over approximately 45 minutes, First Lieutenant Taylor and his wingman continued to make low-level, danger-close attack runs on the surrounding enemy positions.

When enemy fire increased from the village of Ap Go Cong, he requested artillery rounds with lower illumination altitudes be fired on that portion of the village so that the burning rounds ignited the enemy positions.

With both Cobra gunships nearly out of ammunition and the enemy still closing in on the patrol team, First Lieutenant Taylor flew the patrol team's potential ground evacuation route, founding it – finding it unviable based on the heavy enemy ground fire encountered.

Returning to the patrol team's location, he continued to circle it at a low level under intense enemy fire, employing his searchlight to make fake gun runs on the enemy positions to distract them from the patrol team.

Running low on fuel and with the patrol team nearly out of ammunition, First Lieutenant Taylor decided to extract the team with his two-man Cobra helicopter gunship – a feat never before accomplished.

He directed his wingman to fire their remaining minigun rounds on the patrol team's east flank. First Lieutenant Taylor then fired his own last minigun rounds on the enemy positions, opening an avenue of movement to the east for the patrol team.

He directed the patrol team to move 100 yards towards the extraction point, where First Lieutenant Taylor, still under enemy fire, landed his helicopter and instructed the patrol team to climb aboard anywhere they could.

With the four-man, long-range patrol team seated on rocket pods and skids, he evacuated them to the nearest friendly location, undoubtedly saving their lives.

First Lieutenant Taylor's conspicuous gallantry, his profound concern for his fellow soldiers, and his intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty are in keeping with the highest traditions of military service and reflect great credit upon himself, his unit, and the United States Army.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/speeches-remarks/2023/09/05/remarks-by-president-biden-at-presentation-of-the-medal-of-honor-to-army-captain-larry-l-taylor/|title=Remarks by President Biden at Presentation of the Medal of Honor to Army Captain Larry L. Taylor|publisher=The White House|date=5 September 2023|access-date=6 September 2023|archive-date=6 September 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230906024713/https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/speeches-remarks/2023/09/05/remarks-by-president-biden-at-presentation-of-the-medal-of-honor-to-army-captain-larry-l-taylor/|url-status=live}}{{PD-notice}}</ref></blockquote>
